summary: Silver nitrate is a topical caustic (escharotic) and antiseptic supplied as caustic applicator sticks (typically 75% silver nitrate with 25% potassium nitrate) and as topical solutions of varying strength. On contact with tissue it precipitates surface proteins, forming a dense film of coagulated albumin that limits deeper penetration while chemically destroying superficial tissue and acting as a germicide. It is used by clinicians to cauterize wounds, sluggish ulcers, and epistaxis and to remove granulation tissue and warts. Prolonged or extensive use can cause permanent gray-black staining of skin and tissue (argyria); inappropriate use causes chemical burns.

Removal of granulation tissue and warts

Cauterization of vaginal or cervical ulcerations and rectal fissures

moa: Silver nitrate is a caustic escharotic. On contact with tissue, silver ions precipitate cellular and surface proteins, producing a dense film of coagulated albumin (an eschar) that both destroys the superficial tissue being treated and limits penetration into deeper layers. The released silver ions also bind microbial proteins and nucleic acids, giving a powerful chemical germicidal effect. Chloride ions in tissue convert silver nitrate to insoluble silver chloride, which contributes to the characteristic black staining.

absolute: Use on broad areas of denuded or thin, delicate skin where excessive absorption or burns may occur
relative: Neonates and infants (thin, delicate skin; greater risk of burns and methemoglobinemia)
monitor: Treated site for chemical burns or over-cauterization
Skin and mucosa for gray-black discoloration (argyria) with prolonged use
Signs of methemoglobinemia with extensive use, especially in neonates

preg: There are no systemic safety data for silver nitrate in pregnancy. When used topically for cauterization, systemic absorption is minimal and clinically significant fetal exposure is not expected. Use only as needed for the local indication.
lact: There are no data on silver nitrate in human milk. Topical application produces minimal systemic absorption, so effects on a breastfed infant are not expected. Avoid application to the breast or nipple in a nursing mother.
renal: No dosage adjustment is needed for topical use because systemic absorption from intact application sites is negligible. Extensive application to large denuded areas could in theory increase systemic silver exposure.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment is needed for topical use because systemic absorption is negligible.

major: No clinically significant systemic drug interactions with topical use
moderate: Sodium chloride and other chloride-containing solutions precipitate silver as silver chloride and inactivate silver nitrate at the application site
minor: Other topical caustics or astringents applied to the same site may increase tissue injury
interactions.diagnostics: Causes black staining of skin and tissue that may interfere with visual assessment of the treated area

common: Local black/gray staining of treated tissue
Mild local irritation at the application site
serious: Chemical burns from inappropriate or excessive use
Argyria (permanent slate-blue to gray-black discoloration) with prolonged or large-area application
Over-cauterization with damage to surrounding healthy tissue
rare: Methemoglobinemia (particularly with extensive use in neonates)
emergency: Extensive chemical burn or signs of methemoglobinemia (cyanosis, dyspnea, altered mental status) - stop use and seek emergency care

monitoring: Treated lesion for adequate cauterization without excessive injury
Surrounding skin for chemical burns or unintended staining
Cumulative exposure to limit risk of argyria with repeated treatment

counsel: This medicine is applied by a clinician to a specific lesion and is for external use only
Expect the treated area and contacted skin to turn black; this staining is usually temporary on the surface
Do not allow the product to contact the eyes
Report increasing pain, blistering, or spreading skin damage, which may indicate a chemical burn
Keep applicator sticks in a dry, dark place; moisture and light degrade the tip
pk: Immediate local coagulation/eschar formation on contact
Local effect during application; no meaningful systemic peak with topical use
Not characterized; systemic absorption negligible with topical use
Local effect persists until eschar sloughs; staining may persist for days to weeks
Store in a dry, dark place to protect applicator tips from moisture and light
pearls: Applicator sticks are typically 75% silver nitrate with 25% potassium nitrate
The potassium nitrate moderates the reaction and supports the stick matrix
Tissue chloride converts silver nitrate to insoluble silver chloride, producing the characteristic black stain
Saline irrigation inactivates silver nitrate, useful to stop the caustic action
Strength of action is controlled by dilution, contact time, and treated area - keep applications focal
missed: This is not a self-administered scheduled medication. Cauterization is performed by a clinician and repeated only as clinically indicated; a planned re-application that is missed should simply be rescheduled at the next clinical visit.
overdose: Topical overdose presents as chemical burns and extensive black staining. For eye exposure, rinse with lukewarm water for at least 15 minutes; for skin exposure, wash thoroughly with soap and water. If ingested, give milk or water and seek medical care; do not induce vomiting. Extensive exposure can cause methemoglobinemia, treated with methylene blue. Contact Poison Control (1-800-222-1222).
